passage: In Siddiq's Toronto classroom, Ms Reyes held up a card with three lines on it. "Which one matches this line?" she asked, pointing to a fourth. Siddiq, ten, could see it was C, clearly. But one by one, the kids in front said "B." Tuan said "B." Even Maya, the smartest girl, said "B." Siddiq's face went hot. Was he seeing wrong? He looked again: C. Now it was his turn, and twenty faces turned toward him. His mouth went dry. If he said C, they'd laugh. "B," he said quietly. Ms Reyes smiled and explained: everyone before him had been told to say B on purpose, as a lesson. The answer was C. Siddiq stared at his desk. He'd been right all along, and he'd still said B.

qa.q: Which line did Siddiq see was the match?
qa.a: He could see it was C, clearly.

qa.q: Why did Siddiq say "B" when he saw C?
qa.a: Siddiq felt anxious and exposed, afraid the class would laugh if he disagreed with everyone.

qa.q: What could Siddiq tell himself next time he sees something different from the group?
qa.a: Siddiq could remind himself that his eyes are evidence too, and that saying what he sees is worth a moment of awkwardness.

qa.q: How might Tuan have felt saying "B" on purpose while watching Siddiq?
qa.a: Tuan might have felt a bit guilty or curious, watching Siddiq struggle with an answer everyone knew was wrong.

grounding: A child sees everyone pick the same wrong answer and follows the group even though the truth is visible, afraid of being laughed at.

passage: At the school science club in Madurai, the teacher placed two potted plants on the table. "Which one got more sunlight this week?" Lakshmi, nine, had watered them every day. She knew the left one had stood by the window. But Bhavna, the club captain, said, "Right one, obviously," and everyone agreed, nodding and giggling. "Lakshmi?" the teacher asked. Lakshmi's cheeks burned. The others were looking. She thought of the window, then of Bhavna rolling her eyes. "Right one," she mumbled. The teacher checked the logbook. "Actually, the left one. Lakshmi, you watered them. Didn't you notice?" A few children laughed after all. Lakshmi wanted to disappear. She'd been laughed at anyway, just for the wrong reason.

qa.q: Where had the left plant stood?
qa.a: The left one had stood by the window.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling when the teacher asked her?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt embarrassed and anxious, her cheeks burning because disagreeing with Bhavna and the group felt risky.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could Lakshmi try next time?
qa.a: Lakshmi hid what she knew to avoid being laughed at; next time she could say what she saw calmly, since her evidence was real.

qa.q: How might Bhavna have felt when the logbook showed she was wrong?
qa.a: Bhavna may have felt embarrassed too, having led everyone to the wrong answer.

grounding: A child sees the group choose an answer she knows is wrong and follows it, afraid of being laughed at, even though the truth was visible.

passage:
Monday: In class five, the teacher wrote "recieve" on the board and asked if it was spelled right. Everyone shouted "Yes!" Bhupen, ten, was sure it was "ei," but Zubin next to him shouted "Yes!" too. Bhupen said "yes," quietly.
Wednesday: In the spelling test, Bhupen wrote "receive," the way he'd always known. He felt a knot of worry. What if they were all right and he was wrong?
Friday: Marks came back. Bhupen got it right. The teacher said, "On Monday I misspelt it on purpose. Only three of you got it right in the test, but nobody said so out loud." Zubin grinned sheepishly. Bhupen went red. He had known, and still he'd said yes.

qa.q: How did the teacher write the word on the board?
qa.a: The teacher wrote "recieve" on the board.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling on Wednesday during the test?
qa.a: Bhupen felt a knot of worry, doubting his own knowledge because the whole class had said the wrong spelling was right.

qa.q: What could Bhupen do next time he disagrees with the class?
qa.a: Bhupen could say "I think it's ei" out loud, trusting what he knows even if the group says otherwise.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel when the teacher revealed the trick?
qa.a: Zubin looked sheepish, perhaps embarrassed at how easily he'd shouted yes with everyone.

grounding: Over a week, a child follows the class in accepting a misspelling he knows is wrong, worried about standing out, then learns he was right.

passage: After the movie, Indu's friends spilled out of the Pune multiplex, buzzing. "Best film of the year!" said Vijay. "That ending!" everyone agreed. Indu, fifteen, had found it slow and confusing; she'd checked the time twice. She opened her mouth to say so, then closed it. Six faces, all glowing. Maybe she'd missed something. On the auto home they replayed scenes, and Indu laughed at the right moments. By the time she got home, she was telling her mother it was "really deep." Lying in bed, she tried to remember what she'd actually thought during the film. She couldn't quite find it anymore. Had she changed her mind, or had she just gone quiet so long that her own opinion had faded?

qa.q: How many times had Indu checked the time during the film?
qa.a: She'd checked the time twice.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling lying in bed?
qa.a: Indu felt confused and unsure, unable to tell whether she had truly changed her mind or just gone quiet.

qa.q: What could Indu try next time she disagrees with friends?
qa.a: She could say something small and honest, like "I found it slow, but the ending was good," so her own view doesn't fade.

qa.q: How might Vijay react if Indu said she found the film slow?
qa.a: Vijay might be surprised but could accept it, and might even admit a slow part himself.

grounding: A teenager whose friends unanimously praise a film begins to doubt her own view and adopts theirs, unsure whether she truly changed her mind.

passage:
"Did you see Rina's dress today?" Parveen giggled at the lunch table. "So old-fashioned."
"Totally," said three girls at once.
Neelam looked across the canteen. Rina sat alone, eating quickly. Neelam had thought the dress was pretty. Her Nani had one like it.
"Neelam? Right?"
"Um... I guess."
"And she talks like a teacher."
"Yeah," someone said. Everyone laughed.
Neelam laughed too, a beat late.
After lunch, walking back, Parveen linked arms with her. "You're quiet today."
"Just tired."
"Rina's weird, na?"
Neelam hesitated. She actually liked how Rina explained maths. But now she wasn't sure. Maybe they were right. "Maybe," she said. That night, she noticed she'd started to see the dress their way. And she didn't like how easily it had happened.

qa.q: What did Parveen say about Rina's dress?
qa.a: Parveen said it was "So old-fashioned."

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling when she laughed a beat late?
qa.a: Neelam felt uneasy and unsure, going along with the group despite her own opinion.

qa.q: What small step could Neelam take to keep her own view?
qa.a: Neelam could say one honest thing, like "I thought the dress was nice," or sit with Rina some day.

qa.q: What might lunchtime be like for Rina?
qa.a: Rina probably feels lonely and excluded, eating quickly by herself.

grounding: A teenager in a group that looks down on a classmate starts to doubt her own kinder view and adopts theirs, uneasy at how easily it happened.

passage: In class nine, everyone in my group decided Rashida was a show-off. She answered every question, wore a science-fair badge on her bag. At first I didn't agree. I thought she was just keen. But they rolled their eyes every time she spoke, and I started rolling mine too. Then, slowly, I began to actually see her as annoying. When she won the quiz, I heard myself say, "Obviously." It wasn't until the next year, when I was paired with her for a project and she spent hours helping me understand circuits, that I realised: I hadn't really changed my mind. I'd just borrowed theirs. Sometimes I truly agreed with the group. That time, I'd just stayed quiet until I forgot what I thought. I'm Ojas, and that still bothers me.

qa.q: What did Rashida wear on her bag?
qa.a: She wore a science-fair badge on her bag.

qa.q: How does Ojas feel now about going along with the group?
qa.a: Ojas feels bothered and a bit ashamed, knowing the dislike was borrowed rather than truly felt.

qa.q: What helped Ojas see Rashida clearly, and what does that suggest?
qa.a: Working with her on a project showed Ojas who she really was, suggesting that direct experience can break a group's borrowed opinion.

qa.q: How might Rashida have felt in class nine?
qa.a: Rashida likely felt judged and isolated, with a whole group rolling their eyes at her.

grounding: A teenager looks back on adopting a group's dislike of a classmate, recognising it was going quiet rather than a real change of mind.

passage:
Dear Farhan bhai,
Something interesting happened in our class debate today and I keep thinking about it.
The topic was whether we should have a longer school day. Everyone in class, and I mean everyone, voted no. Then Sir asked if anyone disagreed. Silence. I actually thought a longer day with sports might be good, but I didn't say it.
Then Anjali raised her hand and said, "I think it could help if the extra hour was for sports or clubs." The class stared. But within a minute, Deepak said, "Actually, I agree." Then two more. By the end, the vote was almost half-half.
It was like one person broke a spell. I noticed I'd only needed one other person to feel brave. Next time I want to be the Anjali.
Wasim

qa.q: What did Anjali suggest the extra hour could be for?
qa.a: She said it could help if the extra hour was for sports or clubs.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel during the first silence?
qa.a: Wasim felt hesitant and afraid to speak, even though a longer day with sports seemed good.

qa.q: What does Wasim learn from watching Anjali?
qa.a: One person voicing doubt makes it much easier for others to speak honestly, so being that first voice can help everyone.

qa.q: How might Anjali have felt when Deepak agreed with her?
qa.a: Anjali likely felt relieved and supported after the stares, no longer alone in her view.

grounding: A student notices that once one classmate voices a different view, others quickly dare to disagree, showing how one ally breaks group pressure.

passage: Amandeep, you asked how the council vote went. It was so strange. I'm Himani, and I was watching from the side as a class rep. The head boy proposed we spend the whole budget on a DJ for the fest. Everyone clapped. The teacher asked, "All agreed?" Hands went up everywhere. I saw a few people half-raise theirs, looking around. Then Tara from class eleven said, very calmly, "I think we should keep some for the library corner." For a second it was silent. Then someone else said, "Yeah, the books are falling apart." Then another. Suddenly six hands were up for the library. It was like they'd all been waiting for one person to go first. The DJ still got most of the money, but the library got some too. I've never seen a room change so fast.

qa.q: What did Tara say they should keep some money for?
qa.a: Tara said they should keep some for the library corner.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling while watching the half-raised hands?
qa.a: Himani felt curious and a little tense, sensing people were hesitant and waiting for someone else to disagree first.

qa.q: What does this vote show about speaking up in a group?
qa.a: It shows that once one person voices doubt, others quickly feel safe to follow, so a single ally can change a room.

qa.q: How might the people who half-raised their hands have felt after Tara spoke?
qa.a: They likely felt relieved and braver, finally able to support what they really thought.

grounding: A student watches a council vote change once one person voices doubt, showing how a single ally frees others to disagree.

passage: I sit behind Bidisha in the science club, so I saw exactly how it happened. The club leader said our project should be a volcano model. Everybody nodded. I thought a water-purifier would be more useful, but everyone looked so certain. Bidisha had her hand half up, then down, then up again. Finally she said, "Can I ask, would a water filter be more useful for our village?" There was a pause. Then Ramesh, beside me, said, "I was thinking the same thing." After that, three more people agreed. The leader said we'd vote properly. The filter won by two. I can't say what Bidisha was feeling inside, but her ears were red and she kept her eyes on her notebook. I noticed how much easier it was for the rest of us once she'd gone first.

qa.q: What project did the club leader first suggest?
qa.a: The club leader said the project should be a volcano model.

qa.q: How did the narrator feel before Bidisha spoke?
qa.a: The narrator felt hesitant and unsure, preferring the water-purifier idea but holding back because everyone looked so certain.

qa.q: What does the scene show about how one voice affects a group?
qa.a: Once Bidisha asked her question, Ramesh and others felt able to agree, showing that one ally makes honest disagreement much easier.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Bidisha to speak first?
qa.a: Bidisha likely felt nervous and exposed, her ears red, yet her question gave the others courage to agree.

grounding: An observer sees that when one classmate voices doubt about the group's plan, others quickly dare to disagree too.

passage:
"So we're all agreed? We tell the warden to fire the cleaner," said Jaya, looking around the hostel common room. Twenty hands went up.
"I'm not agreed," said Usha.
Twenty heads turned.
"Usha, your earrings went missing too."
"I know. But nobody saw her take anything. We could be wrong."
"Who else would it be?"
"I don't know. That's my point."
Someone muttered, "Always the difficult one."
Usha's face burned. Her hands were shaking in her lap. "I just think we should ask the warden to check first, not accuse."
Jaya sighed. "Fine, write your own note."
Later, in their room, Jaya said, "You made it awkward."
"I know." Usha stared at the ceiling. "I kept thinking maybe I was wrong. But I'd rather be awkward than unfair."

qa.q: How many hands went up in the common room?
qa.a: Twenty hands went up.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling while she disagreed?
qa.a: Usha felt embarrassed and anxious, her face burning and hands shaking, and doubted whether she was wrong.

qa.q: Why did Usha's stand take courage, and what did it risk?
qa.a: Standing alone against twenty people risked being called difficult and making things awkward with friends, but it protected someone from being accused without proof.

qa.q: How does Jaya see Usha's disagreement?
qa.a: Jaya sees it as awkward and annoying, frustrated that Usha broke the group's agreement.

grounding: A young adult who disagrees with an entire hostel group feels stares, pressure and self-doubt, and pays a social cost for standing alone.

passage: I still remember the project meeting in our final year. Kishore, our group leader, wanted to copy a design from an old senior's thesis and just change the colours. Everyone agreed; there were eight of us, and it was the easy route. When he asked, "Any objections?" I heard myself say, "Yes. I think it's plagiarism." The room went silent. Eight pairs of eyes on me. Someone laughed nervously. Kishore said, "Nobody checks." I felt my stomach flip. For a second I thought, maybe I'm overreacting. After the meeting, two people stopped sitting with me at lunch. For a week I felt like an outsider in my own group. Then the professor announced she'd started checking old theses. Kishore didn't say anything to me, but he redid the design. I'm Lakshmi, and I'd say it again, even with the lonely week.

qa.q: How many people were in the project group?
qa.a: There were eight of us.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel after speaking up?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt the stomach flip of self-doubt, then lonely and like an outsider for a week.

qa.q: Why was Lakshmi's objection worth the cost?
qa.a: It stopped the group from submitting copied work, even though standing alone cost Lakshmi friendship at lunch for a while.

qa.q: How might Kishore have felt when the professor announced checks?
qa.a: Kishore likely felt uncomfortable and perhaps embarrassed, realising Lakshmi had been right.

grounding: A young adult looks back on being the lone dissenter in a project group, facing stares, self-doubt and a social cost for speaking up.

passage:
Team coach's note, college debate society, Thursday.
In today's planning meeting, the whole team, eleven members, agreed to argue the "for" side in the national round, because it's easier to prepare. Amandeep alone disagreed. He said the "against" side had stronger evidence and more original arguments. The room went quiet. Tejas, the captain, said, "We've already decided." I watched Amandeep's shoulders go up and his voice get smaller, but he didn't back down: "I just think we'd win more convincingly." Someone rolled their eyes. After the meeting, he sat alone, looking at his notes. I told him that disagreeing with everyone, calmly, took courage, and that I'd ask the team to hear his evidence next week before voting again. He looked relieved, but also tired. Being right doesn't make it easy.

qa.q: How many team members agreed to argue the "for" side?
qa.a: The whole team, eleven members, agreed.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling as his voice got smaller?
qa.a: Amandeep felt pressure and self-doubt, his shoulders rising, yet he held his view.

qa.q: What did the coach do that could help Amandeep?
qa.a: The coach acknowledged his courage and arranged for the team to hear his evidence before voting again.

qa.q: How might Tejas have seen Amandeep's disagreement?
qa.a: Tejas seemed to see it as an obstacle to a decision already made, wanting to move on quickly.

grounding: A young adult who disagrees with his whole debate team feels stares, pressure and self-doubt, and his stance costs something even when he may be right.

passage:
"So we launch the new app in March. Everyone agreed?" Mahima looked round the conference room.
Heads nodded. Mridul hesitated, then said, "Can I ask a question before we decide?"
"Sure."
"The beta testers found the payment page crashed twice in ten tries. I checked the logs last night. Are we fixing that before March?"
A pause.
"It's a minor bug," someone said.
"It might be. But if it happens with real customers, we lose trust. I could be wrong about the scale. Can we get the test team to check this week?"
Mahima frowned, then pulled up the logs on the screen. "Hm. That's more than I thought."
"I'm not against March," Mridul added. "I'd just like us to be sure."
"Okay," Mahima said slowly. "Test first, then decide. Good catch."

qa.q: How often did the payment page crash for beta testers?
qa.a: The payment page crashed twice in ten tries.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling when she pulled up the logs?
qa.a: Mahima felt surprised and a bit concerned once she saw the problem was bigger than she thought.

qa.q: How did Mridul disagree with grace?
qa.a: He checked the logs first, asked a question rather than attacking, gave evidence, and said he might be wrong about the scale.

qa.q: How might the person who called it "a minor bug" feel after the logs came up?
qa.a: They might feel a little embarrassed but also relieved the issue was caught before launch.

grounding: A young professional checks the evidence, then politely raises a different view with a question and data, staying open to being wrong.

passage: A year ago, in my second month at the agency, our director Rehana presented a campaign idea for a school-uniform brand, and the whole room loved it. I had a doubt. The ad showed children rushing through breakfast, and our research said parents were worried about kids skipping meals. I spent that evening re-reading the research to check I wasn't just being difficult. The next morning I asked, "Could I share one point from the parent survey? I might be wrong, but I think the breakfast scene could put parents off." I showed the chart. There was a pause. Rehana studied it. "Hm. What would you change?" "Maybe show them eating quickly but together." She nodded. We changed it. I'm Manjula, and I learnt that disagreeing doesn't have to mean fighting.

qa.q: What did the ad show children doing?
qa.a: The ad showed children rushing through breakfast.

qa.q: How did Manjula feel before raising the doubt?
qa.a: Manjula felt uncertain and a little anxious, worried about being difficult, and so re-read the research to be sure.

qa.q: What made Manjula's disagreement effective?
qa.a: Manjula checked the reasoning first, asked politely, showed the chart, and admitted possibly being wrong, which kept the discussion open.

qa.q: How might Rehana have seen Manjula's input?
qa.a: Rehana seemed curious and open, asking what Manjula would change instead of defending the original idea.

grounding: A young professional checks the reasoning, then politely offers a different view with evidence, staying open to being wrong.

passage:
Team lead's note, design review, Monday.
The whole team was ready to approve the new school-bus route map. Preeti, our junior planner, asked to speak before the vote. She said she'd walked the route on Sunday and found that one stop was on a blind curve with no footpath. She showed photos on her phone, and said, "I might have missed a reason it's placed there. Could we check?" Two senior planners looked annoyed. But the photos were clear. I asked Shalini from road safety to review the stop. She confirmed the danger. We've moved the stop fifty metres to a safer spot. Preeti stayed calm and didn't gloat when she was proved right. I've asked her to present her walking-check method at next week's meeting.

qa.q: How far was the stop moved?
qa.a: The stop was moved fifty metres to a safer spot.

qa.q: What might Preeti have been feeling as the two senior planners looked annoyed?
qa.a: Preeti was probably nervous, but she stayed calm and steady, trusting the photos she had taken.

qa.q: Which parts of Preeti's approach are worth copying?
qa.a: She checked the route herself, gave clear photo evidence, asked politely whether she had missed something, and didn't gloat when proved right.

qa.q: How might the children using the bus be affected by Preeti speaking up?
qa.a: The children would be safer, no longer waiting at a stop on a blind curve.

grounding: A young professional checks the facts, then politely states a different view with evidence, staying open to being wrong.

passage:
Preschool note, Tuesday.
Harish (5) brought a packet of biscuits today. At snack time, his younger brother Asif came over from the toddler room, and Harish immediately gave him two, then broke another in half so they'd have the same. Later, a new boy visiting with his mother sat at the table and looked at the packet. Harish held it close and ate slowly, not offering. When I asked him to share, he gave one, a little reluctantly. I'll try pairing Harish with the visiting child in a game tomorrow so they get to know each other before snack time.

qa.q: How many biscuits did Harish give Asif first?
qa.a: Harish immediately gave him two.

qa.q: What does Harish holding the packet close suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests Harish felt protective of his biscuits and wary of the new boy, whom he didn't know yet.

qa.q: Why is pairing Harish with the visiting child in a game a good idea?
qa.a: Getting to know the boy may make him feel less like a stranger, so Harish may share more easily.

qa.q: How might the visiting boy have felt watching Harish?
qa.a: The visiting boy may have felt left out and shy, wanting a biscuit but new to the group.

grounding: A young child shares biscuits readily with his brother but is slower to share with a visiting stranger's child.

passage: In the courtyard of their house near Thrissur, Joseph, five, sat with a ripe mango. When his big brother Siddharth came home from school, Joseph ran to him and held out a juicy piece. "For you, chetta!" Then he took a slice to Appachan, his grandfather, on the veranda. But when the neighbour's visiting nephew, a boy Joseph didn't know, peeped over the wall, Joseph turned his back and ate quickly. Appachan called, "Share one with the guest, mone." Joseph handed over the smallest slice, frowning, then ran back to sit close to Siddharth.

qa.q: What did Joseph call Siddharth when he gave him mango?
qa.a: He said, "For you, chetta!"

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling when the visiting boy peeped over the wall?
qa.a: Joseph felt wary and possessive, not yet trusting the boy he didn't know.

qa.q: How could Appachan help Joseph share more freely?
qa.a: Appachan could invite the visiting boy to sit with them, so Joseph gets to know him and sees him as less of a stranger.

qa.q: How might the visiting nephew have felt getting the smallest slice?
qa.a: The nephew may have felt a little unwelcome and awkward, being new and given the smallest piece.

grounding: A young child readily shares mango with his brother and grandfather but is slower to share with a visiting stranger's child.

passage: In their Amman flat, Rania, five, was eating date cookies on the rug. Her baby brother Alejandro crawled over, and she put a cookie right into his hand. Then she carried one to Teta in the kitchen. Later, Mama's friend came with her little girl, whom Rania had never seen. The girl sat on the rug and looked at the plate. Rania pulled it closer and turned away. "Rania, share," Mama said softly. Rania held out one cookie, arm straight, not looking at the girl. Then she scooted over to sit by Alejandro.

qa.q: What did Rania put into Alejandro's hand?
qa.a: She put a cookie right into his hand.

qa.q: How can you tell Rania felt unsure about the visiting girl?
qa.a: She pulled the plate closer, turned away and held out a cookie without looking, showing she felt wary of a stranger.

qa.q: What might help Rania feel more generous toward the visitor?
qa.a: A short game together first could help Rania see the girl as a friend, not a stranger.

qa.q: How might the visiting girl have felt?
qa.a: The visiting girl may have felt shy and left out in a new home, being handed a cookie so stiffly.

grounding: A young child shares readily with her brother and grandmother but is slower to share with a visiting stranger's child.

passage: That morning Chandrika, ten, and her little brother Chintu had fought over the last jalebi, and she'd told him she'd never talk to him again. In the afternoon, walking back from the village school past the pond, she saw a bigger boy from the next lane holding Chintu's slate high above his head. Chintu was jumping and crying. Chandrika didn't think. She marched straight over, stood between them and said, "Give it back. Now." Her heart hammered; the boy was a head taller. Her friend Yusuf came and stood beside her. The boy shrugged and dropped the slate. Chandrika picked it up, wiped it on her frock, and took Chintu's hand. At home they told Amma at once. Amma listened, then walked with them to the boy's house to speak to his parents before dinner.

qa.q: What was the bigger boy holding above his head?
qa.a: He was holding Chintu's slate high above his head.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling as she stood between them?
qa.a: Chandrika felt protective and scared at once, her heart hammering because the boy was a head taller.

qa.q: What did Amma do that helped?
qa.a: Amma listened and went with them to speak to the boy's parents before dinner, so the bullying was dealt with the same day.

qa.q: How might Chintu have felt when Chandrika stepped in, after their morning fight?
qa.a: Chintu likely felt relieved and protected, perhaps surprised his sister came to help after saying she'd never talk to him again.

grounding: A child who quarrelled with her brother that morning fiercely defends him from a bully, showing family loyalty overriding a grudge.

passage: At breakfast in their Berlin flat, Selin, eleven, had screamed at her younger brother Tariq for using her hairbrush on the dog. "I hate you!" she'd said. At the school playground that afternoon, she saw three older boys pushing Tariq against the fence, calling him "baby." Something hot rose in her chest. She dropped her bag and ran over. "Leave him alone!" One of the boys laughed. Selin's legs were shaking, but she stepped closer. "I'll get Frau Weber right now." They backed off. Tariq's lip was trembling. Selin put an arm round him, marched him straight to Frau Weber and told her everything. The teacher listened, took the boys' names, and phoned their mother before home time. On the walk home Tariq whispered, "You said you hated me." Selin shrugged. "I do. Only I'm allowed to."

qa.q: What were the older boys calling Tariq?
qa.a: They were calling him "baby."

qa.q: What was Selin feeling when something hot rose in her chest?
qa.a: Selin felt fiercely protective and angry, strong enough to override her morning resentment.

qa.q: Why was taking Tariq to Frau Weber straight away a good choice?
qa.a: It brought in an adult who could stop the bullying the same day and contact their mother.

qa.q: How might Tariq have felt when Selin put her arm around him?
qa.a: Tariq probably felt safe and relieved, and perhaps touched that his sister defended him despite the morning fight.

grounding: A child who quarrelled with her brother that morning fiercely defends him from bullies, showing family loyalty overriding a grudge.

passage: At the Pune school's bus stop, Sarika, nine, stood apart from her twin brother Mintu. They'd fought that morning over who got the window seat, and she wasn't speaking to him. Then a group of older kids started snatching Mintu's cap and throwing it between them. Mintu's face crumpled. Sarika's grudge vanished. She pushed through, grabbed the cap in mid-air, and said loudly, "Stop it. He's my brother." Her classmate Francis stood next to her. The older kids muttered and moved away. Sarika handed Mintu the cap. Then she went straight to the bus conductor aunty and told her what had happened. The aunty wrote down the older kids' names and said she'd tell the class teacher that afternoon. On the bus, Sarika gave Mintu the window seat.

qa.q: What were the older kids throwing between them?
qa.a: They were throwing Mintu's cap between them.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling when Mintu's face crumpled?
qa.a: Sarika felt protective and angry, her grudge vanishing as loyalty took over.

passage: Hemant, you asked why I get upset about family favours. Let me tell you. I'm Vijay mama, and when I was twenty, my uncle was on the village road committee. There was a contract to build the new road. Three contractors bid. One had built good roads for years. But my uncle gave it to his wife's brother, who'd never built anything. At home everyone praised my uncle for "looking after family." I felt proud, honestly. Family comes first; that's what we were taught. But when the road cracked after one monsoon, and a bus got stuck, I saw the other contractor standing by it, shaking his head. I understood then. My uncle's loyalty was real, but so was the harm. A whole village paid for one family's favour.

qa.a: It showed him the real cost of favouritism, that loyalty to family harmed the whole village when merit was ignored.

qa.q: How might the experienced contractor have felt watching the bus stuck?
qa.a: The contractor likely felt frustrated and sad, knowing he could have built a better road.

grounding: An elder recalls seeing an uncle favour a relative for a road contract, understanding family loyalty but also the harm to fairness.

passage: The college union election was two days away, rain had flooded the campus lanes, and Gargi, nineteen, was volunteering at the nomination desk. She understood the pull; she'd seen her own mother help relatives with jobs. But it wasn't fair. At the next volunteers' meeting, she raised it calmly: "We should apply the deadline equally." passage: Lalit, you think loyalty means covering for family? Let me tell you. I'm Vandana, your father's elder sister. When I was twenty-five, I worked as an accountant at a cooperative bank.
